title: Charts and exhibits: stage 6 of a case interview
description: Exhibits test whether you can find what matters, and many cases turn on them. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Charts arrive in almost every case. You have a minute or so to make sense of one and say what it means. Here is a simple way to do that every time.
body:
Stage 6 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why it matters

Exhibits test whether you can find what matters, and many cases turn on them.

The common mistake

Describing the chart instead of drawing an insight from it.

What to do, and what to say

Take a moment

Ask for 30 seconds. Read title, axes, units and footnote. Write down two insights before you speak.

"Thank you. May I take a moment to process this?"

Insights, not description

Find what matters, connect parts of the chart, do the maths without being asked, and link back to the goal.

"Two things stand out. First... Second... Given our goal, the second matters more, and I’d like to quantify it."

If stuck or wrong

Say it out loud. Silence reads as panic; a structured step back reads as composure.

"I’d like to take a step back. We know A, B and C, and we’re trying to get to X."

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

The interviewer hands you a dense chart.

Show a strong answer

"Thank you. May I take a moment to process this?" Then read title, axes, units and footnote.

Why it works: Thirty seconds of reading prevents the usual chart mistakes.

You’ve read the chart. Start your answer.

Show a strong answer

"Two things stand out. First, demand overtakes supply from 2028. Second, the gap reaches 20% by 2030. Given our goal, the second matters more, and I’d like to quantify it for our client."

Why it works: Insights with numbers, prioritised, linked to the goal.

You realise your reading of the chart was wrong.

Show a strong answer

"I’d like to take a step back and re-examine this. We know A, B and C, and we’re trying to get to X."

Why it works: Correcting yourself calmly reads as composure, not failure.

Next stage: maths.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. All ten stages, with every phrase, are on the free perfect casing page.
